definition: Elements of a case are the component parts of a legal claim or cause of action that a plaintiff must prove to succeed in a lawsuit. Each claim is made up of specific elements, and the plaintiff must establish each one to prevail. In civil cases, the burden of proof is generally a preponderance of the evidence, meaning it is more likely than not that the element is satisfied. For example, the elements of a negligence claim are:  The existence of a legal duty owed by the defendant to the plaintiff  A breach of that duty by the defendant  Cause in-fact or actual cause, i.e., plaintiff’s injury would not have occurred but for the defendant’s conduct.  Proof that the defendant’s breach caused the injury (often defined through proximate cause)  Damages, meaning the plaintiff suffered actual, compensable harm such as physical injury, financial loss, or property damage When filing a civil lawsuit, a plaintiff sets out the cause of action and alleged violations in a complaint. In a negligence claim, this would include allegations that the defendant owed a duty, breached it, that the breach was the proximate cause of injury, and that damages resulted.
